items.headline: Seven biotechs driving progress in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
items.preview: This article highlights seven biotech companies advancing treatments for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). Each company is developing innovative therapies to address this severe genetic condition.
items.article:
Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a severe genetic disorder caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene, leading to muscle degeneration. Recent years have seen significant therapeutic advancements, with several drugs entering the market and many more in clinical trials. This article explores seven biotech companies making strides in DMD treatment, including Sarepta Therapeutics, Wave Life Sciences, and Solid Biosciences.

Why this matters: These companies are at the forefront of developing therapies that could significantly improve the quality of life for individuals with DMD, a condition that affects one in 3,500 male births worldwide. Their innovative approaches, ranging from gene therapies to small molecules, represent hope for patients and families affected by this debilitating disease.

items.headline: BU/VA Researcher Honored for Contributions to Trauma Psychology
items.preview: Colleen Sloan, PhD, has received the Outstanding Contributions to Practice in Trauma Psychology award for her impactful work in trauma-focused mental health care.
items.article:
Colleen Sloan, a clinical associate professor at Boston University, has been awarded for her significant contributions to trauma psychology, particularly in developing effective interventions for trauma-related conditions. Her work emphasizes the importance of culturally responsive care and the adaptation of evidence-based interventions for underserved populations.

Why this matters: Recognizing leaders in trauma psychology like Sloan highlights the critical need for effective mental health care strategies that address the unique challenges faced by individuals with trauma histories, particularly among marginalized groups.

items.headline: Digital detective: sleuthing on (and safeguarding) the natural world with dPCR
items.preview: Digital PCR (dPCR) is revolutionizing environmental monitoring by enabling precise detection of invasive species and biodiversity assessment.
items.article:
Digital PCR (dPCR) has emerged as a powerful tool for environmental monitoring, allowing for the precise detection of nucleic acids in various ecosystems. Recent studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in identifying invasive species and assessing freshwater biodiversity through environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis.

Why this matters: The ability to accurately monitor invasive species and biodiversity is crucial for conservation efforts, as it enables timely interventions to protect ecosystems from harmful invaders and supports sustainable management of natural resources.

items.headline: UCB’s pipeline strategy in 2026: Doubling down on immunology and neurology
items.preview: UCB is focusing its pipeline strategy on immunology and neurology, aiming for innovative therapies that address underlying disease mechanisms.
items.article:
UCB is strategically enhancing its pipeline in immunology and neurology, concentrating on innovative therapies that go beyond traditional approaches. The company has made significant acquisitions to bolster its capabilities in these areas, including cell therapy and T-cell engagement technologies.

Why this matters: UCB's focused strategy aims to deliver next-generation therapies that could transform treatment paradigms in autoimmune and neurological diseases, potentially improving patient outcomes and establishing the company as a leader in these therapeutic areas.

items.headline: The gut takes it all: Enteroendocrine control of developmental growth
items.preview: A new study reveals how the gut regulates growth in response to nutritional stress, highlighting the role of enteroendocrine cells.
items.article:
Research published in PLOS Biology uncovers the role of enteroendocrine cells in the gut as key regulators of growth during nutritional stress in Drosophila larvae. The hormone Limostatin (Lst) produced by these cells suppresses insulin signaling to slow development under nutrient scarcity.

Why this matters: Understanding the mechanisms by which the gut influences growth can provide insights into developmental biology and potential therapeutic targets for growth-related disorders in other organisms, including humans.
